title: Comparison & Logical Operators
objective: Write comparisons with strict equality and combine them with && / || / ! to form boolean expressions.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A comparison asks a yes-or-no question about two values and produces true or false. JavaScript actually has two kinds of equality check: === (strict equality) compares both value and type without converting anything, while == (loose equality) tries to convert the two values to a common type first, which can produce surprising results like "5" == 5 being true. Always prefer === and !== — they do what you expect.

<, >, <=, and >= compare size the same way you'd expect from math class. A single = assigns a value to a variable; a double or triple equals sign compares two values — mixing them up is one of the most common early bugs.
You can combine comparisons with &&, ||, and !. && is true only when both sides are true. || is true when at least one side is true. ! flips a boolean's value, turning true into false and back again.
explanation.rule: Use === and !== for comparisons — they check type as well as value, unlike == and != which silently convert types.

examples.title: Strict vs Loose Equality
examples.note: === sees a number and a string as different, so it's false. == converts "5" to a number first, so it's true — this is exactly the surprise === avoids.

feedback.correct: Correct — === checks type as well as value, and a number is never strictly equal to a string.
feedback.incorrect: === never converts types. A number and a string, even with the 'same' digits, are not strictly equal.

assignment.title: Ready to Forge
assignment.brief: Write isReady(temperature) that logs true if temperature is at least 1200 and at most 1500, otherwise logs false, using &&.
requirements: Use >= and <= combined with && to check the range.
Log the resulting boolean with console.log().

hints: You need both temperature >= 1200 and temperature <= 1500 to be true.
console.log() can log a boolean value directly — no conversion needed.
1300 is within the range, so the result should be true.
